title: Clones Win by Fate, Not Speed

scenes.tts: Why is this oesophagus still healthy? Researchers sequenced normal oesophagus from nine deceased organ donors. In middle-aged and elderly donors, Notch one mutant cells made up an estimated twelve to eighty percent of the lining. Notch one mutations also turn up in oesophageal cancers. Yet this tissue looked normal, and the mutations were more common here than in tumours.

scenes.tts: The lining stays the same size only if cell gain matches cell loss. In mouse oesophagus, only the basal progenitor cells divide. Each division gives two progenitors, two differentiating daughters, or one of each. In wild-type tissue, these three outcomes are balanced. Differentiating cells move upward and are shed.
scenes.visual: stack of layers with basal progenitors dividing; three division outcomes drawn; balance beam; differentiating cells rise and are shed
scenes.narration: The lining stays the same size only if cell gain matches cell loss. In mouse oesophagus, only the basal progenitor cells divide. scenes.tts: A mutant clone wins by tilting that balance. Did the mutant cells simply divide faster, or did their daughters differentiate less? Notch signalling is linked to differentiation of squamous epithelial cells. In mouse oesophagus, Notch one mutant clones expanded without a higher division rate. Tracking was consistent with more progenitor daughters and fewer differentiating ones.
scenes.visual: a mutant clone grows in the basal layer; two question cards, faster division is crossed out, fewer differentiating daughters is ticked

scenes.tts: Count the progenitors one division makes: two times the chance of two progenitors, plus the chance of one of each. Balanced odds are zero point two five, zero point five, and zero point two five. That gives one, so the count holds steady. Now tilt the odds to zero point three five, zero point five, and zero point one five. Then the average becomes one point two.
scenes.visual: three bars for the three outcomes at 25, 50, 25 with the sum; bars tilt to 35, 50, 15 and the result changes from 1.0 to 1.2
scenes.caption: Count the progenitors one division makes: two times the chance of two progenitors, plus the chance of one of each. Balanced odds are 0.25, 0.50, and 0.25. That gives one, so the count holds steady. Now tilt the odds to 0.35, 0.50, and 0.15. Then the average becomes 1.2.

scenes.tts: Start with one hundred progenitors and no cell death, in a simple model. Each generation multiplies the count by one point two, with no change in cycle time. After three generations, you expect one hundred seventy-two point eight progenitors. The model shows that fate alone is enough, and the mouse tracking was consistent with that.
scenes.visual: a bar of 100 progenitors grows through three multiply-by-1.2 steps to 172.8 while a cycle-time tag stays unchanged

scenes.tts: A cancer gene mutation did not make this tissue malignant. In mouse oesophagus, wild-type neighbours at the clone edge differentiated faster. In a mouse model, early lesions were removed more often when the surrounding clones were highly competitive. That is a mouse result, not human prevention data. So ask which clones expand, and why, not only which mutations a tissue carries.
